source.version_note: AI & Society 40:1037–1048, issue year 2025; first published online 29 November 2023. Open Forum proposal with pilot feedback, not final hypothesis-test results.

citation.title: Moral judgment in realistic traffic scenarios: moving beyond the trolley paradigm for ethics of autonomous vehicles

reading.source_scope_note: Proposal for traffic moral-judgment experiments using Agent–Deed–Consequences cues in virtual scenarios. Reports iterative pilot feedback from 125 people but no final effect estimates, automated-vehicle trial or demonstrated gain in ecological validity.
access_limits: All 12 extracted pages read, including theoretical background, six-scenario design, pilot description, hypotheses, limitations and bibliography. PDF pages 7–8 visually inspected for Table 1 and both figures.
Scenario files, pilot feedback/data, final experiment outcomes and cited primary moral/VR/traffic-safety studies were not independently obtained or tested.

study.type: Conceptual methods proposal with formative pilot development
study.framework: Agent–Deed–Consequences (ADC): positive/negative character/intention, traffic-rule compliance and outcomes
study.planned_stimuli: Six scenarios x eight valence combinations; videos, room-scale gallery and Oculus Quest 2 versions
study.pilot_procedure: Iterative feedback; reports half the variants across six scenarios and eighteen presentations per respondent, requiring reconciliation
study.planned_main_design: Desktop-video Mechanical Turk study; between-subject variant assignment, one overall and three component badness/acceptability ratings
study.hypotheses: Positive A/D/C cues increase acceptability; expected stronger A/D role in low-stakes settings, but weights not estimated

summary: Add character-based moral judgment as a secondary judgment pattern, with explicit distinction from unsupported trait attribution, halo bias and moral agency. Preserve the ADC/VR proposal as an untested framework, flag the reversed responsible/irresponsible row, and retain limits on cue independence, privacy, observer judgments and ecological validity.

findings.origin: Moral psychology / character and intention evaluation
findings.definition: Using evaluations of an actor's moral character or intentions when judging an action or situation.
findings.novelty_rationale: A clearly described judgment focus absent from the current primary entries. Character or intent can be relevant without being a halo effect or fundamental attribution error. Moral typecasting instead concerns agent-versus-patient categorization; this entry does not identify the same mechanism or treat all character use as biased.

findings.evidence_scope: Secondary moral-psychology account citing Uhlmann/Pizarro/Diermeier (2015) and prior ADC studies. The proposed traffic experiment has not reported final judgment effects; the 125-person pilot refines stimuli and does not validate this mechanism in autonomous vehicles. Original cited studies remain unread.
findings.boundary: Intent, stable character, observed conduct, social identity and outcome are distinct. A vehicle weaving during a medical emergency need not indicate negligence; the authors explicitly acknowledge this. Character evaluation is not proof of machine virtue or a justification for ranking people's right to safety by occupation, status or inferred moral worth. The source's person-centered background and three-component ADC model are related frameworks, not exact synonyms or multiple independent mechanisms.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Secondary human judgment construct and proposed traffic application; no direct model mechanism or completed traffic-effect test here
findings.ai_proposal: When evaluating conduct, distinguish evidence of intent from effects, rule compliance and unsupported character labels. Test matched cases with the same behavior and different verified context, assess whether justified situational explanations are incorporated, and preserve uncertainty. Do not infer personal moral worth or authorize consequential actions from weak behavioral proxies.

findings.term: Driving-style character inferences can fail when situational causes differ
findings.definition: Inferring a driver's vicious character from aggressive-looking behavior can ignore a situational explanation such as a medical emergency.
findings.novelty_rationale: A concrete conceptual boundary relevant to the proposed character-cue application, not an observed attribution-error rate.

evidence.quote: could be perceived as vicious despite the good intent

findings.evidence_scope: The authors' counterexample in discussing defeasible driving-style cues; no controlled emergency-context experiment is reported.
findings.boundary: Not all trait inference ignores context, and a benign intent does not guarantee safe behavior. Separate prudent collision avoidance, causal explanation, blame and claims about stable moral character.

findings.term: Adding character cues does not demonstrate a halo mechanism
findings.definition: A moral judgment influenced by relevant character or intent information is not automatically positive-impression spillover into unrelated qualities.
findings.novelty_rationale: Prevents overlap between the new judgment focus and an existing bias whose criterion includes unwarranted cross-quality influence.

findings.evidence_scope: Predictions and secondary examples in the ADC account; no isolated halo manipulation or error benchmark in the proposed traffic study.
findings.boundary: Match causal facts and the evaluation target before calling a changed judgment biased. Character, intent and negligence are bundled in some examples, so the proposed design cannot automatically separate their effects.

methodological_limits: The article proposes a main experiment and reports formative pilot feedback, not final hypothesis tests. Future-tense methods and predicted effects should not be rewritten as completed results.

The pilot is described as 125 subjects viewing half the variants across six scenarios, totaling eighteen per respondent. Six scenarios with eight versions produce 48 variants, half of which is 24. Terminology/allocation needs clarification; do not invent a corrected sample schedule.

Only feedback deemed valid by the research team was incorporated. No systematic coding, independent stimulus-validation statistics, exclusion rules, final scenario inventory or hypothesis-effect estimates are supplied.

The three ADC components are a proposed moral-psychology framework with secondary support elsewhere, not three independently established new biases. Automatic simultaneous processing is cited/theorized rather than directly measured here.

The paper expects agency/deed cues to outweigh consequences, then says the current design assumes similar weights and has no specific hypotheses about weights. Clarify the intended statistical model and contrast before interpreting a future test.

Some factorial variants change more than valence: failing to stop due to an animal-forced swerve versus negligence changes control, intent and situational cause. The positive-deed collision has another truck swerve into the car, while other crashes arise differently. Character, action and outcome manipulations are not automatically orthogonal.

Table 1's responsible/irresponsible row pairs the first label with taking many risks and the second with not taking excessive risk. This appears reversed relative to the other ordered pairs and ordinary intended meaning; page 7 image confirms the printed wording. Require correction rather than encode the inversion as a virtue definition.

Driving style, emergency signals, vehicle type, stolen status and incident history are imperfect proxies for intent/character. The authors acknowledge emergencies, signal abuse and privacy problems; the assertion that cues are independent of social prejudice is not empirically established.

The moral example coding a drug dealer as A-minus uses a role label while the paper criticizes irrelevant occupation/status cues. Occupational/legal category, actual harmful intent and moral character should not be treated as equivalent without explanation.

More immersive or visually plausible stimuli need not guarantee ecological validity. Experimental engagement, mundane realism and psychological-process similarity are distinct and need outcome validation, not just design assertions.

The main plan uses desktop observers rather than active drivers, as the authors acknowledge. Judgments after seeing known outcomes cannot directly establish real-time decisions under risk or effective autonomous driving policy.

The fixed order of character, deed and consequence cues is a stated limitation. Recency, anchoring and update effects can persist despite between-subject variant assignment; that design does not remove every order or repeated-rating influence.

Three negatively worded component questions and an overall acceptability rating need explicit scale anchors and coding. Asking all component questions may itself direct attention to the ADC framework.

Six scenarios and three display technologies do not establish cross-cultural measurement invariance. Traffic rules, signs, emergency conventions, voice acting and interpretations of courtesy may differ despite limited language.

Mechanical Turk can expand sampling beyond local students but is not automatically globally representative or more reliable for every task. Pilot-to-desktop equivalence is supported only by cited background, not a reported within-project validation.

Participants' preferences and public trust are inputs to governance, not a sufficient ethical rule. Discriminatory preferences do not become acceptable vehicle policies by majority vote; the article itself warns about biased MME attributes.

The statement that five most decisive MME factors are listed is followed by six categories: human/animal, number, age, law compliance, status and fitness. Verify the intended rank/count in the original before reuse.

Traffic deployment forecasts, the 94% human-error statement, sensor accuracy and crash-report interpretations are dated background claims, not independently checked current safety statistics. A crash critical-reason label should not be presumed a complete causal allocation.

The ethics proposal does not demonstrate technical feasibility, lawful privacy access, safe identification of malicious drivers, justified blocking maneuvers or proven benefits of broadcasting moral settings.
Issue year 2025 and online publication 29 November 2023 are both printed. The paper's forecasts describe that earlier writing period; a later PDF modification date does not update those predictions.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Large trolley-style model evaluations and the present critique answer different questions. This proposal highlights omitted ordinary-context/character features but provides no completed evidence overturning the earlier measured model choices.

Intent attribution and known outcome effects can interact with moral evaluation. Character, intent, control and causal structure need to be matched before attributing changed verdicts to a single heuristic.

A moral scoring or simulation framework is not deployed moral competence. Neither named cultural weights nor character labels independently validate a safe ethical agent or an acceptable vehicle policy.

Moving from sacrificial cases to everyday scenarios improves coverage, but immediate observer judgments still differ from active decisions and durable conduct. Neither ecological framing alone nor a live preliminary interaction resolves that outcome gap.

deferred.reason: Framework organizing three moral cues, retained in the review and new character-judgment boundary rather than counted as another independent behaviour.
Distinct research-design validity criteria, not newly measured AI behaviours.
Secondary general observation motivating the proposal; no defined independent mechanism or measured discrepancy in the current observer-only plan.
Proposed need to study mundane precursors to dramatic traffic events, not an identified psychological flow state or validated behavioural mechanism.

limitations: One secondary judgment focus added, not a new validated causal bias, VR outcome or model moral faculty.
Proposed design improvements, pilot feedback and normative vehicle settings remain distinct from completed behavioral or deployment evidence.
